deep.reconstruction:
The page has two unrelated blocks. Block A (top) is number theory. Block B (bottom) is a step in Gauss's fit of Pallas's orbit to six oppositions. It continues directly into the next page, 'Pallaselemente aus den 6 Oppositionen'. The material on the previous page reaches 1811, so the sheet probably dates from about 1811.

A. Partial Euler products. Heading: Σ log(p/(p-1)).
(1) Exact running products. Gauss multiplies 2·(3/2)(5/4)(7/6)(11/10)(13/12) = 1001/192. He then multiplies by (17/16)(19/18) to get 1001·17·19/(192·16·18) = 323323/55296. The small fractions 2/1 … 17/16 are written over the headline. The numbers 576 and 2304 at the top are probably auxiliary denominators (576 = 3·192, 2304 = 4·576); unsure.
(2) Natural logarithms. ln 1001 = 6.90875478 and ln 192 = 5.25749537, so ln(1001/192) = 1.65126 (entry '13. 1.65126'). He adds ln(p/(p-1)) for p = 17, 19, 23, 29, 31, 37: 0.060625, 0.054067, 0.044452, 0.035091, 0.032790, 0.027399. Their sum is 0.254424. This gives Σ_{p≤37} ln(p/(p-1)) = 1.90568 (entry '37 1.90568').
(3) Briggsian (base-10) logarithms. log10 323323 = 5.5096366 and log10 55296 = 4.7426937. Their difference, 0.7669429, is log10 of Π_{p≤19}.
- He tabulates 10^7·log10(p/(p-1)) for p = 23…53: 193051, 152400, 142404, 118992, 107239, 102172, 93401, 82726. These sum to 992385, giving 0.8661814 for Π_{p≤53}.
- He does the same for p = 59…97: 74240, 71785, 65309, 61603, 59904, 55325, 52642, 49073, 45005. These sum to 534886, giving 0.9196700 for Π_{p≤97}.
(4) Summary table, x : Π_{p≤x} p/(p-1) : ln x : third column.
- 19 : 5.847 : 2.94 : 0
- 53 : 7.3482 : 3.97 : −0.59
- 97 : 8.3113 : 4.57 : −0.83
The products are the antilogs of the step (3) values. The middle column is the natural log of x.
- My interpretation of the third column: it is Π − 2 ln x. This gives −0.59 and −0.83 exactly; for 19 it gives −0.03, written as 0.
- In effect Gauss compares the Euler product with a multiple of log x. The ratios Π/ln x are 1.99, 1.85, 1.82, falling toward e^γ ≈ 1.781. That is Mertens' third theorem, Π_{p≤x} p/(p−1) ~ e^γ ln x.
- No constant is stated on the page. The pair 0.0065917, 0.0011160 / 9.7867252, 1081156 is not explained by me.

B. Pallas: radius vectors and heliocentric latitudes at six oppositions (1803–1811). Each column is one opposition and uses the osculating elements for that date (given on the next page).
(1) Mean motion. n (″/day) = 770.7255, 770.7928, 770.1373, 770.5010, 770.1580, 768.2969.
(2) Semi-major axis by Kepler's third law with the planet's mass neglected: log a = (2/3)(log k″ − log n).
- The constant 3.5500066 is log10 of the Gaussian constant k = 3548.18761″.
- Rows: log n (2.8868997, …), log(k/n) (0.6631069, …), log a (0.4420713, …).
(3) Semi-latus rectum: log p = log a + 2 log cos φ, with e = sin φ.
- The row 270040, 269248, 268880, 268362, 267090, 262916 is −2 log cos φ in units of 10^-7. It is twice the next page's 135020, 134624, …
- Result: log p = 0.4150673, 0.4152715, 0.4154043, 0.4153194, 0.4155755, 0.4166936.
(4) Radius vector. The row 9.8917947, … is log(1+e cos v); the next page has e cos v = −0.22054, …, +0.15367, …
- log r = log p − log(1+e cos v) = 0.5232726, 0.5155612, 0.3533230, 0.4492234, 0.5370545, 0.4722233.
(5) Heliocentric latitude from the observed geocentric latitude b at opposition. Sun, Earth and planet then lie in one plane perpendicular to the ecliptic. The law of sines gives sin(b−β) = R sin b / r.
- The row 9.8673677, 9.4176831, … is log(R sin b). For column 1 this implies R ≈ 1.017, i.e. an opposition in late June (1803), consistent with heliocentric longitude 277°.
- Subtracting log r gives log sin(b−β). Rows: b−β = 12°45′32.02″, …; b = 46°26′36.00″, …; β = b − (b−β) = +33°41′3.98″, +10°27′7.82″, −33°40′26.88″, +28°14′58.71″, +27°20′16.43″, −4°53′5.32″.
(6) Residuals. The next page gives β from the elements (sin β = sin i sin u): +33°41′6.30″ etc. Differences: −2.32, +2.10, +6.66, +3.83, −17.53, −4.84.
- The last row (−1.00, +4.11, +5.99, +3.98, −15.86, −3.34) is the residuals after the small corrections δi = −1″ and δΩ = −2.5″ written on the next page.
- These residuals feed the least-squares adjustment of i and Ω.
errors: Row 'p=43' in the base-10 table: 10^7·log10(43/42) = 102192, but 102172 is written (if the reading is correct). The sum 992385 uses 102172, so log10 Π_{p≤53} should be 0.8661834 rather than 0.8661814. The effect on 7.3482 is negligible (true value 7.34825).
The entry for 19 reads 5,8473 in the transcription; 323323/55296 = 5.84713. This is probably a misreading of 5,8471, or else a slip in the last digit.

Column 4 latitude: 42°11′25.60″ − 12°56′26.89″ = 29°14′58.71″, but 28°14′58.71″ is written, and the next page has 28°14′54.88″. So the b value should read 41°11′25.60″ (a transcription or pen slip). The final β is consistent.
Column 3 residual: −33°40′26.88″ minus the next page's −33°40′39.54″ is +12.66″, but +6.66 is written. One of the two values is misread (e.g. 32.88″ here or 33.54″ there), or Gauss slipped.
Third column of the prime table: if it is Π − 2 ln x, the entry for 19 should be −0.03 rather than 0. The interpretation is uncertain.

deep.surprise_reason: The Pallas part is routine working material for Gauss's well-documented Pallas orbit project. The prime part shows Gauss numerically tabulating the Euler product Π p/(p−1) up to 97 against log x. This is an empirical precursor of Mertens' third theorem (1874). Gauss's numerical interest in prime distribution is known, but this particular computation is a minor unpublished detail, and no constant e^γ or asymptotic law is stated.
